I can now force specific modules to appear. To do this I first generate the specific bit of grid they need. A large module like this would be highly unlikely to appear by chance on a random grid.

Here's a comparison showing no-, dumb- and hierarchical smoothing. The hierarchical smoothing helps preserve the intent of the input-tiles while smoothing out the jankyness from the weird underlying grid and from the limited slope angles in the input tileset

Yet another light baker. Actually does some ray marching, but still pretty ad hoc. The textures are: 1. Normals (procedurally painted in big chunky strokes) 2. 3D Signed Distance Field 3. 3D Ambient Occlusion in positive and negative X,Y and Z
I'm exploring the Half Edge data structure. Feels like a really lightweight, powerful and versatile way of representing topology. A big thanks to everyone suggesting I look into it.

I only sample my noise texture once per quad, but I scroll the UVs randomly forward or backward along the flow of the smoke. This further breaks up the recognizability of individual blobs and it creates some of that cool multi layered flow feeling thick smoke should have
A somewhat major breakthrough in my procedural generation: a heuristic for deliberately generating navigable levels
If your terrain generator supports overhangs you gotta flaunt it. I don't make the rules, but I do follow them.

Long time fans of the show will not be surprised to learn that this is indeed running on tile based WFC. This time around, I'm getting the best of both worlds by using a mix of triangular and square tiles. (The squares are cut along each diagonal to create 4 triangles though)

For my blood splatter UVs, I'm interpolating between sprite-space and skin-space using the fwidth of skin UV. This gives me a sprite-space map on the tummy (where the skin UVs are static) while the splatter on the face follows the actual motion of the head.
